title: Josiah Seeks God and the Book of the Law Is Found
summary: Josiah, king at eight, begins to seek God as a teenager and then purges idolatry from Judah, Jerusalem, and the northern territories. While the temple is being repaired, Hilkiah the high priest finds the Book of the Law, and when it is read to Josiah he tears his clothes in grief. The prophetess Huldah confirms that judgment will come on Jerusalem but promises that Josiah, because he humbled himself, will not see it; Josiah then gathers the people and leads them in renewing the covenant.
story: Manasseh's long reign and Amon's short one left Judah soaked in idolatry. Josiah is the last great reforming king of David's line, and Chronicles presents him as walking in the ways of David without turning to the right or the left. His reform has two stages: first a young king's personal seeking of God and his cleansing of the land, then the discovery of the Law, which deepens everything. The chapter is shadowed by Huldah's word that judgment is coming anyway. Josiah's reform will delay but not prevent the fall of Jerusalem. Readers who know the ending (chapter 36) feel the poignancy: this is the last bright light before the dark.
historical:
Josiah reigned about 640 to 609 BC. The years given in verses 3 and 8 place his seeking of God around 632 BC, the start of his purge around 628 BC, and the finding of the book in his eighteenth year, commonly dated 622 BC. These were the decades of Assyria's collapse. After Ashurbanipal's death around 631 BC the empire weakened rapidly, and Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. That power vacuum may explain how Josiah could extend his reform into the old northern territories (verse 6). The prophets Jeremiah (who dates his call to Josiah's thirteenth year, Jeremiah 1:2) and Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1) spoke during his reign.

The parallel account in 2 Kings 22 and 23 places the whole purge after the finding of the book; Chronicles begins it earlier and presents the book as the climax. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, identify the book with Deuteronomy or a form of it, because the reform's emphases (one place of worship, the destruction of high places, covenant curses, a Passover at the central sanctuary) match that book closely. Since the early nineteenth century, many critical scholars have argued that Deuteronomy was composed or substantially edited around this time; others hold that an older Mosaic book, long neglected, was recovered. Both views agree that the book's discovery reshaped Josiah's reign.
cultural:
Scrolls could easily be lost in a temple complex with storerooms and treasuries, especially after decades of neglect under Manasseh and Amon. Tearing one's clothes was a public act of grief or horror, the natural response to hearing the covenant curses read aloud and realizing they applied. Consulting a prophet to inquire of the LORD was the proper step when a king needed to know God's will. Huldah, a prophetess living in the Second District (probably a newer quarter of Jerusalem), is consulted even though Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active; nothing in the text treats this as unusual, and her word is received as the word of the LORD.

Burning the bones of priests on their altars (verse 5) permanently defiled those altars, making them unusable for worship. Covenant renewal ceremonies, where a leader read the law aloud and the people pledged to keep it, had precedents in Israel's history: Moses at Sinai (Exodus 24:7), Joshua at Shechem (Joshua 24), and Jehoiada's covenant under Joash (23:16). The king standing "by the pillar" (verse 31) was the customary royal position in the temple court.
literary: The chapter has three parts: the purge (verses 1-7), the repair and discovery (verses 8-21), and the prophecy and covenant (verses 22-33). The word book or scroll recurs ten times, making the discovered text the center of gravity. The scene of discovery is told with an ironic understatement: Shaphan reports on the money first and only then mentions, almost as an afterthought, that Hilkiah has given him a book. Huldah's oracle has two parts, one for "this place" and one for "the king of Judah," separating national judgment from personal mercy. Verse 27 piles up Josiah's responses (a tender heart, humbling himself, tearing his clothes, weeping) and then gives God's answer: "I have heard you." The final verse frames the reform as lasting throughout his reign.

outline.t: Josiah seeks God and purges the land
The Book of the Law found and read

doctrines.note: The recovered book reorders the nation's life. God's written word is shown as something that can be lost, found, read, and obeyed, and that judges even a reforming king's best efforts.
Josiah leads the people in pledging to keep the covenant with all their heart and soul, the language of Deuteronomy 6:5. Covenant renewal is a public, communal act.
Huldah declares that judgment on Jerusalem is settled, yet Josiah personally is spared. God's mercy to the humble does not cancel his justice on a nation's accumulated sin.

words.note: Torah, instruction or law. Though often translated law, the word's basic sense is teaching. The Book of the Law of the LORD is God's instruction for his people's whole life, not only a legal code.
Sefer, scroll or book. Used ten times in this chapter, it names a written document. The repetition makes the chapter a story about the power of a written text rediscovered.
Rakhakh, to be soft or tender. Huldah says Josiah's heart was tender (verse 27): responsive and open, the opposite of the hardened hearts the prophets condemned.
Kana, to humble oneself. Used twice of Josiah in verse 27, it links him with Manasseh's repentance in chapter 33 and with God's promise in 7:14. Humility is what God hears.

christ: Josiah's reform shows both the power of God's word and the limit of reform. The book brought grief, humility, and a covenant, but it could not change the heart of the nation, and within a generation Jerusalem fell. Jeremiah, who prophesied in Josiah's reign, looked forward to a new covenant in which God would write his law on his people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:31-34). The New Testament proclaims that Jesus established that new covenant through his blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13). The pattern of a king reading the scroll to the people also finds an echo in Jesus opening the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth and declaring it fulfilled (Luke 4:16-21). These are thematic connections, not predictions within Chronicles.

hard.q: How could the Book of the Law be lost, and was it really written by Moses?
hard.a: The text says the book was found during temple repairs and attributes it to Moses (verse 14). After Manasseh's long idolatry, it is plausible that copies of the Law were neglected, hidden, or destroyed. Traditional interpreters take the attribution at face value: an ancient Mosaic book, perhaps Deuteronomy, recovered after decades of neglect. Many critical scholars argue that Deuteronomy took its final form in the seventh century BC, whether drawing on older traditions or composed to support the reform, and some see the discovery account as a way of giving it authority. Others propose a middle view, with ancient Mosaic material edited over time. What all readers agree on is the text's claim that when the word was heard, it demanded a response, and the king obeyed.

questions: Josiah began to seek God at about sixteen. What would it mean for young people in your community to be taken seriously as seekers of God?
God's word had been lost in God's own house. What parts of Scripture have been neglected in your life or church, and what might happen if they were rediscovered?
Josiah's tender heart was the reason God heard him. What makes a heart tender or hard toward God?
